extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of comparative religion and mythology; general readers interested in the history and evolution of religion
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and distinguishing the historical types and evolution of deities (animistic spirits, fetishes, totems, ancestor-gods, departmental gods such as sun- and corn-spirits) and the processes by which they gain attributes and cults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animistic conception of spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything natural possesses life and so, probably, 'soul,' 'ghost,' or 'spirit' — souls/ghosts arise from visions and dreams and are early ideas contemporaneous with the dawn of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the idea of spirit is early and pervasive, that spirits explain unseen agencies (winds, dark woods) and that spirit-ideas infuse and spiritualize earlier personalization of objects. Example: the ubiquity of invisible powers causing terror and prompting offerings. Use this criterion to identify earliest stage beliefs where natural phenomena are regarded as inhabited by spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fetish (personal familiar) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The fetish is a personal familiar — a spirit attached to a human being that is acquired by a person or family for luck and which requires worship, sacrifice, and feasting; it generally inhabits an object of peculiar shape or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes manufactured or adopted objects (carved figures, stones, bones, necklaces, stuffed skins, dried hands). Fetishes may be bought, sold, loaned, or inherited and are not necessarily tutelary deities. Example: Samoyede _sjadaei_ and household _Hahe_. Use these markers when classifying a cult-object as a fetish rather than a higher god.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of making and using fetishes
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of making a fetish is almost universally the same: select an object resembling a head/figure or curiosa, clothe/embellish it, carry or place it in a special receptacle, smear its mouth with oil or blood, and set offerings before it when its aid is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical signs: dedicated sledge or resting place (_hahengan_), ritual smearing, offerings of food. Use these procedural signs to identify typical fetish cult practice; examples from Samoyede and other hunter groups are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offerings to spirits: libation and combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Spirits are conceived as substantial beings nourished by food and drink; to send offerings to invisible powers there are two methods: libation (liquids evaporating into air) and combustion (solids burnt so smoke reaches spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why blood, fat, smoke, fermented liquors, perfumes and clothing are offered. Gives ethnographic examples (Veddah blood offerings, Peruvian fat-sacrifices). Use these technical distinctions when analyzing sacrificial practice and its logic (volatilisation to reach invisible beings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful fetish → criterion for elevation to godhead
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'successful' fetish survives domestic/test use, proves to be a luck-bringer or performs marvels, and through these acts or the policy of its devotees may become a god.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only fetishes that 'survive the test of experience' are cherished and can evolve; unstable or useless fetishes are abandoned. Example terms: _t'raphim_, _penates_. Use 'survivability' and demonstrated efficacy as markers of potential progression from fetish to household god or wider cult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totem-origin indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Totemic spirits achieve godhead similarly to fetishes; indicators include animal likenesses/attributes in deities, ritual devouring or substitution of animal/man for the eponym, and retention of animal insignia even after anthropomorphization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egyptian animal-headed deities, Grecian Athene's owl, Aztec humming-bird cloak for Uitzilopochtli. Use iconographic remnants (fur, feather, animal head) and sacrificial/ritual practices (communal eating/consumption of totem) to infer totemic origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancestor-worship as path to deity
rubrics_metrics.description: The dead man may be worshipped by his descendants because of his personal might, memory, or the duty of care; over generations the memory grows legendary and miraculous, converting a man into a deity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track processes: sons tending manes, cult at tombs, miracles at shrines, legendary accretion making birth/death supernatural. Examples: Egyptian, Chinese, Indian cases and the continuity of ancestor cult in China. Use presence of genealogical cult, filial obligations, and shrine miracles to identify ancestor-to-god evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact with the gods (reciprocal contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early man enters a tacit pact with gods: 'Feed us, send us plenteous game, O Divine One, and we shall in turn maintain thee with sacrifice' — religion as reciprocal contract rather than mere belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes functional/contractual nature of worship: offerings are payment for divine assistance. Compare hunter vs agricultural compacts (blood-sacrifice continuity). Use evidence of transactional rites and cultic reciprocity to interpret religious motives and types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental (functional) deities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain deities are 'departmental' (god of fire, wine, hunting, thunder, crafts) — this character becomes definitive particularly in higher polytheism where gods preside over specific functions or domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that departmental names may be objectionable but occur historically; relate to social/economic specialization. Use attribution of specific spheres of influence and specialized rituals as criteria for classifying a deity as departmental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsistence-driven religious change (nomadic→agricultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change from nomadic/hunting to agricultural life gives birth to new religious ideas (corn-spirit, earth/water/sun personifications), alters the compact with gods, and leads to different sacrificial practices (often more systematic blood/vegetal offerings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cults: hunter's fetish/utility rituals vs husbandman's crop-focused contract and tithe/victim offerings. Use shifts in primary ritual objects (game to grain), cult frequency, and severity (e.g., human sacrifice in Mexico) to date or explain religious transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corn-spirit to god evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The corn-plant was conceived as having a genius or informing soul; in agricultural societies the corn-spirit attains prime importance and may evolve into major deities with expanded attributes (e.g., Osiris: corn-spirit → guardian of agriculture → judge of the dead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iconography (stalks of corn from Osiris' body), ritual cycle (seasonal festivals, sowing/winnowing analogues), and later moral/judicial functions indicate elevation. Use agricultural centrality, seasonal myths, and ritual symbolism to identify corn-spirit origins and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun-god typology: animistic vs anthropomorphic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the animistic idea of the sun itself as a living god and the anthropomorphic 'man of the sun' or culture-hero dwelling in the sun; both concepts can coexist or be distinct within a mythology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Greek Apollo (culture-hero) vs Helios (sun itself); Egyptian multiple deities aboard a solar boat; Babylonian Merodach and Japanese Ama-terasu as animistic solar deity. Use textual/iconographic evidence to determine whether the solar cult worships the luminary itself or an anthropomorphic office/agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical evolution of gods
rubrics_metrics.description: Though early gods may be savage or immoral like their worshippers, over time gods acquire ethical qualities (justice, wisdom, mercy) as human desires and institutions (monasticism, contemplation) shape divine attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe later texts where deities are repositories of justice/wisdom (e.g., Egyptian Ra, Osiris, Thoth) and compare earlier mythic portrayals. Use institutional evidence (temples, priesthoods) and literary evolution to trace moralization of deities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution for myth-interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: No single interpretive key (linguistic, solar, vegetable, etc.) should dominate mythological conclusions; employ multiple rational methods and avoid mono-causal explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit advice: 'Let no method, linguistic, solar, anthropological, dominate our conclusions, but let none be absent.' Use interdisciplinary evidence (linguistics, ritual, iconography, comparative ethnography) to support interpretations and guard against over-simple theories.
